name: PT Solusi Bangun Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Solusi Bangun Indonesia: a cement asset the exchange will not let you trade
frontmatter.summary: Indonesia's listed cement arm of Semen Indonesia sells almost all its output back to its own group, earns a mid-single-digit return on equity and has a free float below the exchange's floor. Its shares have been suspended and BEI now lists the company among issuers at risk of forced delisting, with voluntary delisting, a rights issue or a SIG share sale under consideration. Fundamental value sits below the last print; under the house rule a suspended stock is NOT RATED.
thesis: The data pack understates the business: its depreciation slice is not the real charge, so restated from the LK (IDR660.3bn for FY2025) FY2025 EBIT is IDR1,092.3bn and EBITDA before right-of-use depreciation is IDR1,752.7bn at a 16.3% margin [S2, S11].
Adding right-of-use depreciation of IDR114.5bn gives the company's own FY2025 EBITDA of IDR1,870.0bn, so the restatement reconciles to the audited accounts rather than to a data vendor [S2, S11].

Volume and price are turning: 12.1 Mt of cement and clinker in FY2025 and 9.2 Mt in the first nine months of FY2026, with revenue of IDR8,480.0bn in that period against a full-year build of IDR11,451.5bn [S11, S4].
The industry is structurally oversupplied at 122 Mt of installed capacity against 66.0 Mt of consumption, so price is set by the marginal funded tonne and exports are the only release valve [S6, S8].
Value is asset-backed but return-poor: the plants were appraised at IDR30,573.2bn against a book value of IDR15,429.0bn, yet ROE is 4.3% against a cost of equity of 12.6% [S20, S2].

The equity is untradeable and its terminal form is a live binary: Semen Indonesia owns 83.5%, 91.2% of revenue is earned from related parties, the free float is 1.1%, the shares are suspended, and BEI's delisting watchlist sits alongside three corporate options [S2, S9, S16, S14].

catalysts.event: The suspension reaches the exchange's two-year forced-delisting threshold, the trigger BEI has already flagged to the market
FY2026 audited accounts, the first full year under the transformation programme and the test of whether the margin held through the price war
FY2026 dividend decision at the annual meeting; the payout has been about half of profit and is the only cash route to shareholders
Government housing and infrastructure programmes move from budget into construction, the demand swing the industry itself cites for next year

blocks.text: **NOT RATED**. That is the house rule, not a view about the cement business: the constitution defines NOT RATED for suspended or insufficient-data names, and SMCB has not traded since the free-float round, with no three-month ADTV and repeated zero-volume sessions [S0, S16]. For reference, our fundamental value after the house liquidity discount is Rp724 against a last traded price of Rp775, a total return of -2.4% including a dividend of Rp32 [S0]. On the rating scale alone that return would be HOLD; the suspension rule overrides it. No position can be established or exited, so the target is a marker, not an exit.

The larger point is that the register itself may not survive in its current form. The exchange's delisting-watchlist announcement of 30 June 2026 lists SMCB among the issuers at risk of forced delisting after a suspension of more than a year, and on 23 July 2026 the company confirmed it is weighing voluntary delisting, a rights issue with HMETD, and a secondary offering of Semen Indonesia's existing shares [S14]. Each option touches the share count or the ownership register differently, and none is decided. A target for the current 9,019m shares is therefore a valuation of one branch of a binary, not a forecast of the register.

What we own at the last print is a cement business with 14.9 Mt of capacity in four integrated plants, 12.1 Mt of cement and clinker sales in FY2025 and revenue of IDR10,737.2bn [S9, S11, S2]. Restating depreciation from the filing rather than the data pack lifts FY2025 EBITDA before right-of-use depreciation to IDR1,752.7bn, a 16.3% margin; adding the right-of-use charge of IDR114.5bn gives the company's own IDR1,870.0bn and turns a falling-profit story into a flat one [S2, S11]. The first nine months of FY2026 already produced revenue of IDR8,480.0bn, net profit of IDR476.7bn and gross profit of IDR1,880.0bn on volume of 9.2 Mt [S4].

The variant view is not that the shares are worth twice the price. It is narrower and, we think, better founded. First, the margin is administratively defended: almost all revenue is earned from the parent and its subsidiaries, so the transfer price does not clear in a spot market running at 122 Mt of capacity against 66.0 Mt of consumption [S2, S6]. That is a governance problem and a stability feature at the same time. Second, the asset base is worth more than its carrying value: the group's own appraiser put the fixed assets at IDR30,573.2bn against a book value of IDR15,429.0bn [S20, S2]. Third, the balance sheet is nearly unlevered, with net debt of IDR1,648.6bn and net debt to EBITDA of 0.9 times at FY2025, and bank loans already down to IDR1,142.8bn at 30 June 2026 [S2, S3].

Against that, the business earns 4.3% on equity in our forecast year against a cost of equity of 12.6%. A company that earns below its cost of capital is worth less than its book unless it grows, and it cannot grow much: national capacity is roughly double consumption [S6]. That is why our primary method produces Rp867 a share, the EV/EBITDA cross-check Rp1,201 and the book-value cross-check Rp806; the weighted value of Rp1,028 before the liquidity discount reflects those three [S0].

The two things that move the value are therefore not commodity price and not volume. They are the transfer price the parent pays for cement, and whether the exchange restores a trading line. A higher related-party price on the same tonnes would lift every year of the forecast; a rights issue, a controller sell-down or a delisting would change the share count and the register at the same time [S2, S16, S14].

PT Solusi Bangun Indonesia is the listed cement arm of the Semen Indonesia group, formerly Holcim Indonesia, renamed in 2019 after the state group bought the Holcim stake [S2]. It runs four integrated cement plants — Narogong in West Java, Cilacap in Central Java, Tuban in East Java and Lhoknga in Aceh through its subsidiary Solusi Bangun Andalas — with total cement capacity of 14.9 Mt and 1,750 people [S9]. Alongside cement it sells ready-mixed concrete under the Dynamix brand, aggregates from its own quarries, and waste-management services that feed alternative fuel into its kilns; the ready-mix and aggregate businesses sit in wholly owned subsidiaries, Solusi Bangun Beton, Readymix Concrete Indonesia and Pendawa Lestari Perkasa, and are small relative to the cement book [S2, S9].

The revenue model is simple and, for a commodity producer, unusually intermediated. Cement and clinker tonnes are sold at an average realised price, and the group reports a single consolidated revenue line of IDR10,737.2bn for FY2025 on 12.1 Mt of sales [S2, S11]. What matters for the equity is who buys: 91.2% of FY2025 revenue was earned from related parties, overwhelmingly from Semen Indonesia itself and its trading and regional subsidiaries [S2]. SMCB is, in substance, a production subsidiary with a listing.

Strategy since the second half of FY2025 has been a group-led transformation: operating efficiency, alternative fuels, tighter marketing and distribution, and a return to regional brands — the company brought Semen Kujang back to West Java — alongside an export push [S11, S4]. The export channel is the strategic novelty. A dedicated terminal at Tuban, a project of the parent group, supports up to 1.0 Mt a year of cement exports, and the company has a partnership with Taiheiyo Cement for the west coast of the United States [S8, S4]. Exports began in June 2026 and were running by September [S4]. That is a run-rate well inside the terminal's capacity; in the base case the terminal reaches only about two thirds of its capacity by FY2030, and the remaining export headroom is a bull-case driver rather than an assumption [S4, S8].

The footprint is a genuine asset: two plants inside the Java market, where most Indonesian cement is consumed, plus East Java for the export berth and Aceh for the Sumatra market [S9]. That geography matters more than brand in a commodity. It is also why the company can run at a high rate of utilisation while the industry as a whole cannot: our base case has volume of 13.8 by FY2030 against 14.9 Mt of installed capacity, without a new kiln [S9].

Cement is a regional business before it is a national one, because the product is heavy, cheap per tonne and
expensive to move overland. Plants earn their returns from the radius they can serve by truck, which is why a
producer with capacity inside the main island of Java is structurally better placed than one shipping clinker
across the archipelago. Ports change that calculus only for clinker and for export markets, and only where a
dedicated berth removes the handling cost.

The controlling shareholder is PT Semen Indonesia (Persero) Tbk with 83.5% of the shares, and the company remains consolidated in a state-owned group that also owns Semen Padang, Semen Tonasa and Semen Baturaja [S9, S2]. Group membership is the source of both the offtake and the governance discount that this report has to price. No segment disclosure is granular enough to split cement from ready-mix profit, and we do not attempt to; the consolidated economics are the only ones the filings support [S2].

Indonesia can make far more cement than it consumes. Installed capacity is about 122 Mt a year against domestic consumption of roughly 66.0 Mt, an overcapacity rate approaching half the industry's installed base on its own arithmetic [S6]. The consequence is that price is set by the marginal tonne, and the marginal tonne is increasingly funded by new entrants that compete on volume rather than return [S6, S17]. National production fell in FY2025 to 64.7 Mt and domestic sales fell, on weaker purchasing power, heavy rainfall that delayed construction and slower infrastructure spending [S5].

FY2026 has been better. The national market grew 7.8% in volume on the association's data as government programmes and a low base lifted demand [S17]. SMCB's own nine-month volume of 9.2 Mt grew more slowly than the market, which means it gave up a little share [S4, S17]. That is the honest reading of the operating data and we carry it into the forecast: our volume grows at the company's own three per cent assumption after the FY2026 actual run-rate, rather than at the market's current rate [S2].

The pricing environment is where the industry's structure bites. Cement prices in Indonesia have been broadly flat for years while costs moved, because no producer can afford to lose volume in an oversupplied market; the industry's answer has been cost, not price [S11, S6]. Our model handles this with a coal link that recovers nine tenths of an input-cost move and leaves the rest in the margin, and with a realised price that escalates at the rate the company itself assumes in its impairment test rather than at spot [S2]. Coal is the single largest variable cost: the ICI4 index the industry buys against was US$40.6/t a tonne on average in FY2025 and is forecast at US$62.0/t this year before easing to US$52.5/t [S0].

Competitive positioning is strong on assets and weak on pricing power. The five forces read badly. Rivalry is severe and structural; buyer power is concentrated in a handful of distributors and, for SMCB specifically, in its own parent; supplier power sits with coal, power and freight; the threat of new entrants has already been realised by new capacity; and substitutes — steel and timber structures — are a slow erosion rather than a shock [S6, S17]. The one force that works in SMCB's favour is the difficulty of building a new integrated plant inside Java: permits, limestone and community consent make brownfield capacity inside the market scarce even when national capacity is not [S9].

Exports are the pressure valve and the growth option. The Tuban terminal supports up to 1.0 Mt a year of cement exports and gives the group a route to the United States west coast through the Taiheiyo partnership [S8, S4]. Export tonnes earn a lower price per tonne than domestic bagged cement but absorb fixed costs, which is why we treat the terminal as utilisation support rather than as a margin story.

Regulation matters in two directions. On the product side, energy and environmental rules raise the cost of the marginal clinker tonne and reward producers with alternative-fuel substitution — SMCB's kilns already burn waste-derived fuel, and the company reports sustainable solutions at a large share of revenue [S4]. On the market side, the exchange's free-float rules now govern whether the shares can trade at all: the minimum free float has been raised to fifteen per cent and issuers below the threshold carry a special notation [S18], and SMCB was suspended in the free-float round [S16]. A suspension of two years or more is itself a delisting trigger under the exchange's delisting rule [S14]. That is a regulatory constraint on the equity, not on the business, but it dominates the investment case.

The cement cycle in Indonesia has run through two full turns since the Asian financial crisis: a building boom
before the global financial crisis, then a decade of capacity additions that outran demand as state
infrastructure spending arrived later and smaller than planned. Producers responded by defending volume, which
is rational for a business with high fixed costs and irrational for the industry's returns. Consolidation has
been the slow answer; the state has done most of it, which is why the largest producer is a state-owned group
and why the listed minorities in that group are small.

The moat, such as it is, is the quarry and the kiln, not the brand. That supports a through-cycle valuation based on assets and cash flow rather than on a growth multiple, and it explains why the discounted cash flow is the primary method and the book-value cross-check is a floor rather than a target [S9, S6].

The first analytical job is to fix the data. The data pack carries a depreciation slice rather than the real charge, because the Indonesian cash-flow statement is presented on the direct method and the pack has taken an operating-expense line instead [S0]. The filing's allocation of depreciation and depletion is IDR660.3bn for FY2025 and IDR664.5bn for FY2024, split across cost of revenue, general and administrative and selling expenses [S2]. We restate the last two fiscal years from the notes and the earlier years from their own filings [S21, S20]. On that basis FY2025 EBIT is IDR1,092.3bn, the LK's own profit before interest and tax, and EBITDA before right-of-use depreciation is IDR1,752.7bn, a 16.3% margin [S2]. Adding the right-of-use charge of IDR114.5bn gives IDR1,870.0bn, which is the company's own stated FY2025 EBITDA and the figure that reconciles our restatement to the audited accounts [S2, S11].

The operating-expense lines are reconcilable line by line. Distribution and selling took IDR977.2bn, general and administrative IDR309.4bn, a foreign-exchange loss IDR30.3bn and other-net IDR7.5bn, which is what takes the LK's gross profit of IDR2,416.6bn to the IDR1,092.3bn before interest and tax we use [S2]. The model routes the exchange loss and other-net to non-operating items and holds them at zero for every forecast year: the rupiah loss is a translation item that reverses with the currency, and other-net has averaged a small net charge with no operating driver [S2, S4]. We state that normalisation rather than bury it, because the pack's own operating-expense line differs from the LK's by a rounding of scope.

Revenue fell -9.2% in FY2025 to IDR10,737.2bn on volume of 12.1 Mt and a weaker mix, while cost of revenue fell to IDR8,320.6bn, holding the gross margin at 22.5% [S2, S11]. Interest of IDR152.6bn — lower as the company repaid bank loans — left pre-tax profit of IDR939.1bn and net profit of IDR658.7bn [S2, S0]. FY2026 reverses the direction: revenue of IDR11,451.5bn in our forecast, up 6.7%, on volume of 12.4 and an average price of 925,000 a tonne, which is the nine-month realised rate carried into the fourth quarter [S4].

The opex line is the correction that matters most. The last actual interim filing shows distribution and selling of IDR619.8bn plus G&A of IDR145.4bn on revenue of IDR5,502.3bn, and the nine-month reported figures imply a similar burden; that ratio, 13.4%, is what we hold [S3, S4]. The step-up from the FY2025 ratio is outbound freight (domestic alone up by a quarter), new export freight and a jump in other distribution costs, while G&A was flat [S3]. We keep the interim run-rate in real terms for all five years, because freight scales with volume and the company's efficiency narrative is not yet visible in the reported line [S3, S4]. This single input is worth more than the rating: at the earlier sub-twelve per cent ratio the model printed a double-digit total return; at the documented ratio it prints -2.4%.

Margins follow from that. We hold the gross-margin input at 22.5%, the FY2025 level, and let the coal link move the printed margin: because ICI4 is forecast at US$62.0/t against a FY2025 average of US$40.6/t, the FY2026E gross margin prints at 21.7% and recovers as the deck's coal price falls [S0, S2]. That is deliberate and it is the arithmetic the reader should see: with nine months at the reported gross profit of IDR1,880.0bn on revenue of IDR8,480.0bn, the full-year print assumes a weaker fourth quarter, not a stronger one [S4]. We assume no fourth-quarter uplift.

The fourth-quarter build therefore runs as follows. FY2026E revenue of IDR11,451.5bn less the nine-month IDR8,480.0bn leaves a fourth quarter priced at the same 925,000 a tonne and the residual volume; operating expenses at 13.4% of that revenue, depreciation at 6.2%, interest at the FY2025 debt cost and tax at the effective rate give FY2026E net profit of IDR579.6bn [S4, S2]. Because the nine-month figure was IDR476.7bn, the implied fourth quarter is below the FY2025 fourth quarter, not above it. The reason is the margin path, not a volume collapse: the nine-month margin was the strong part of the year. A reader who believes the nine-month margin holds through December should treat our FY2026E earnings as conservative and the bull case as the right frame.

Interest is charged on opening debt at a constant rate — the engine's convention, set at the three-year average cost of debt. Because the company is repaying bank loans, that convention overstates interest expense in the outer years and is therefore conservative for value; it does not touch the rating, which the suspension rule sets. Net borrowing is held at zero: the company has funded itself from operations and repaid debt, and any future draw is a financing decision rather than an operating assumption [S2, S3].

The cost base is dominated by energy, freight and maintenance. Coal and coal-linked power are about fifteen per cent of cost of revenue in our model, oil about five per cent, with the balance limestone, quarrying, labour, packaging and distribution [S2]. This is why the model needs a coal link: in a market with 122 Mt of capacity, a producer recovers input-cost inflation through mix and cost programmes, not through list price, and the FY2026 evidence — coal up by half, realised price up a few per cent, margin roughly intact — is exactly that pattern [S4, S11].

Cash generation is better than the profit and loss suggests, but only modestly. FY2025 free cash flow to the firm was IDR805.7bn after capex of IDR388.4bn, a low number because the company deferred discretionary spending during the transformation year [S0, S2]. We fund capex at 6.2% of revenue — the depreciation charge, neither an expansion budget nor a deferral — which produces FY2026E free cash flow of IDR790.2bn [S0]. Working capital is 6.3% of revenue, close to the three-year average; the balance sheet carries IDR1,910.4bn of trade receivables from related parties, which is the great majority of the receivables book, so working capital is a function of the parent's payment behaviour rather than of third-party credit [S2].

The balance sheet is the strongest part of the equity story. At FY2025 total debt of IDR1,863.8bn — bank loans plus lease liabilities — against cash of IDR215.2bn gave net debt of IDR1,648.6bn and 0.9 times EBITDA [S2]. The interim balance sheet already shows bank loans down to IDR1,142.8bn, with lease liabilities of IDR175.8bn, and interest cover is comfortable [S3]. Equity of IDR13,204.6bn gives a book value per share of 1,464 [S2].

Capital allocation is conservative to the point of inertia. The dividend has been about half of profit — 36.5 a share out of earnings of 73 in FY2025, against 41.3 a share the year before — which we carry forward at 50.0% [S2, S0]. Cash not paid out has gone to debt repayment rather than to new capacity, which is the right call in an oversupplied market and the reason net debt has fallen for three years [S2].

On earnings quality, the accruals screen is clean: operating cash flow exceeded net profit in FY2025, so there is no sign of profit running ahead of cash [S0]. The real flag is not accruals but origin. With 91.2% per cent of revenue from related parties and IDR1,910.4bn of trade receivables from them, the reported margin is a transfer price, not a market outcome [S2]. That is disclosed, audited and consistent across years, so we classify it as an optics-class rather than a manipulation-class flag — but it means the earnings are only as durable as group policy. Two smaller points: the company revalues nothing in its accounts (the appraised fair value of IDR30,573.2bn is disclosure for impairment testing, not a revaluation surplus in equity), so book value is historical cost and comparable across years [S20]; and the FY2025 tax charge of IDR280.4bn on pre-tax profit of IDR939.1bn is above the statutory rate, which we hold in the forecast rather than optimise away [S2, S0].

Cement is a long-lived asset business with a commodity price, so the primary method is a discounted cash flow on free cash flow to the firm, at a through-cycle price rather than at spot. We weight it sixty per cent, cross-check with EV/EBITDA at twenty-five and with price to book at fifteen; the weights are the industry card's and we have not overridden them.

The cost of capital is built bottom-up at 11.9%. The house risk-free rate is 7.4%, the mature-market equity premium 4.2% with a country risk premium of 2.5%, and the industry unlevered beta of 0.90 regeared to 1.01 at the company's debt-to-equity of 0.16 gives a cost of equity of 12.6%. Debt costs 9.4% pre-tax and the weights are 85.9% equity and 14.1% debt. Terminal growth is 2.5%, exactly the perpetuity the company uses in its own value-in-use calculation on nominal rupiah cash flow, and well below nominal GDP growth because an industry running at this much overcapacity should not be capitalised for real growth [S2, S6].

The discounted cash flow gives Rp867 a share on an enterprise value of IDR8,788.8bn, with 67.3% of that value in the terminal period. A terminal share near two thirds is normal for a cement plant but it is also the honest measure of how much of this valuation rests on the assumption that after the forecast the business earns its cost of capital in perpetuity. We are explicit that it does not today: ROE is 4.3% against a cost of equity of 12.6%. The terminal value is justified by the asset base and by the related-party price rather than by growth, which is why terminal growth is set near inflation and not above it.

The two cross-checks bracket the answer, and the gap between them is the most informative number in this section. EV/EBITDA at 6.7 times our FY2025A EBITDA of IDR1,752.7bn gives Rp1,201, 38.5% above the primary method. Two things make that reading explicit. First, the multiple is the engine's blend of the peer median and SMCB's own five-year average, not a house target; both components are computed in the valuation workbook, and the peer median sits well below the own-history number because the peers are priced at trough profitability. Second, the metric is FY2025A, not the forecast year an earlier draft implied, and it excludes right-of-use depreciation because we treat the leases as operating costs. The EV/EBITDA leg is therefore the most optimistic of the three and sits outside the engine's divergence limit, which is why we flag the gap here rather than trim the multiple. The discounted cash flow is lower because an 11.9% cost of capital on a business earning 4.3% on equity is a poor trade, and the multiple assumes the asset is worth its through-cycle peer-and-history value regardless of that spread.

Price to book at 0.6 times forward book gives Rp806, -7.1% against the primary. The justified ratio implied by the model's own inputs — sustainable ROE 4.3%, terminal growth 2.5% and cost of equity 12.6% — is a small fraction of book, well below the blend the engine uses. The reconciliation is the asset appraisal: the appraiser put fixed assets at IDR30,573.2bn against book of IDR15,429.0bn [S20], so the accounting multiple we apply is roughly half the multiple it implies on appraised assets. On the appraised base the book leg is close to the justified level rather than above it. That is why we keep fifteen per cent on book: it is a floor struck on conservative carrying values, not a claim that the business deserves a premium to its peer median.

The appraised asset value deserves its own cross-check because it is the strongest upside in the file and the market price ignores it. IDR30,573.2bn of appraised fixed assets less net debt of IDR1,648.6bn gives an asset value several times the market capitalisation of a suspended line; even after a one-third haircut for the industry's overcapacity, the implied equity value sits above our discounted cash flow. We do not put it into the weighted target — an appraised value is not a cash flow and a minority in a suspended, related-party-dominated register cannot force a sale of the assets — but it is the number that would anchor a take-private or a delisting price, and it is why we describe the shares as asset-backed rather than as a value trap.

The sensitivity table shows the two levers that matter: realised price and the coal price, with volume third. The price lever is worth more than the volume lever because a price change meets a cost base that is only partly variable, and the coal lever matters because energy is the only large cost the company does not control. A reader who believes the transfer price is set to leave SMCB with a fixed margin should read the price sensitivity as the one that does not apply; a reader who believes the parent takes whatever margin it needs should read it as the only one that does.

What the market price implies is easier to state than to interpret. At Rp775 the company is valued at 5.0x times our FY2026E EBITDA, 12.1x times our FY2026E earnings and 0.5x times book, with a dividend yield of 4.1% [S0]. Those are the multiples of a stock that cannot be traded, with a controlling shareholder at 83.5% and a free float of 1.1% [S9, S0]. Our fundamental value of Rp1,028 is struck off the same numbers without the suspension, and the 30.0% discount we then apply is the house's standard allowance for an illiquid line, not an estimate of what a forced seller would receive. There is no bridge: we found no post-balance-sheet disposal, rights issue or special dividend to add, and the FY2025 dividend was already paid before the June cash balance [S3, S4].

The share count is a valuation assumption that the reader has to see. We value 9,019m shares with no change in count, because none of the three options the company disclosed is a decided corporate action: a rights issue with HMETD would add shares and dilute the per-share value, a secondary offering of SIG's existing shares would add free float without dilution, and a voluntary delisting would remove the line entirely, at a price nobody has yet named [S14]. The base case is the existing register; the alternatives are the scenario branches in the next section, not facts in the model.

The largest risk is not commercial, it is structural. The shares are suspended because the free float fell short of the exchange's rules, the minimum has since been raised to fifteen per cent with a special notation for issuers below it, and SMCB sits at 1.1% [S16, S18, S0]. The company has now put three remedies on the record: voluntary delisting, a rights issue with HMETD, and a secondary offering of Semen Indonesia's existing shares, against BEI's 30 June 2026 announcement that SMCB is among the issuers at risk of forced delisting after a prolonged suspension [S14]. The register effects are not symmetric. A rights issue at a discount would dilute every per-share figure in this report and would need SIG to backstop it; a secondary offering would fix the free-float test and restore trading without adding a share, at whatever discount the seller accepts; a voluntary delisting would extinguish the line and turn the minority's outcome into a negotiated buyout price, with the appraised asset value of IDR30,573.2bn the only anchor the company has published [S14, S20]. Likelihood: high that the constraint persists into next year, because none of the three has been filed or priced; impact: severe, because the equity cannot be traded at any price.

The second structural risk is the delisting clock itself. The suspension is already past the point where the exchange must tell the market it may delist; the rule allows delisting where a stock has been suspended in the regular and cash markets for two years, and that threshold falls within the life of this target [S14]. A reader who treats the twelve-month target as a tradeable forecast is assuming a remedy that has not been announced.

The industry risk is equally well evidenced. With 122 Mt of capacity against 66.0 Mt of consumption, a demand disappointment restarts the price war and there is no floor under the marginal tonne [S6]. Likelihood: medium in any single year; impact: high. It is worth being precise about the mechanism, because an earlier draft was not: our model's cost base is mostly variable, with cost of revenue and operating expenses both set as shares of revenue, so a price cut does not pass entirely to EBIT — it passes partly, and the sensitivity table is the honest measure of how much. The truly fixed item is the capital stock, which is why a price cut still destroys value without destroying the volume.

The related-party risk cuts both ways and deserves its own line. Almost all revenue is earned from the parent group, so the transfer price is an administrative decision [S2]. Likelihood of a change: low while the group needs SMCB's cash for its own dividends; impact: high in either direction. We do not assume a gift and we do not assume a haircut in the base case. The downside is carried in the bear scenario, which cuts volume and price and takes two points off the gross margin: a transfer-price reset at the top line plus the freight and coal squeeze takes the value to Rp847 against a base of Rp1,028 [S2, S4]. The receivables are the second channel: IDR1,910.4bn owed by related parties is a working capital exposure, not an earnings one, so an extension of payment days is a one-off cash use that the balance sheet absorbs rather than a recurring charge we would capitalise [S2].

Macro and currency risks are real but second-order. Coal is priced in dollars and the rupiah has moved from 16,448 to a forecast 17,570, so an imported cost rises in rupiah terms even when the dollar index is flat [S0]. Our coal link is calibrated on the dollar index and the observed FY2026 margin, so the currency path is embedded in the margin rather than modelled as a separate lever; a further depreciation would hit cost of revenue before it reached price [S2, S4]. Interest-rate risk is minor: bank loans are down to IDR1,142.8bn and falling [S3].

Operational risk is the ordinary cement risk — a kiln outage, a quarry permit, a coal-supply interruption — and it is manageable because the company runs four plants and can reallocate production [S9]. Governance risk is covered in the next section; the short version is that a minority holder here has no vote that matters and no exit.

Scenario probabilities of 25.0% bear, 50.0% base and 25.0% bull reflect a business whose price is administered by the group, not a coal miner's spread. The bear is now a real test rather than a rounding: cuts to volume and price, a two-point gross-margin squeeze from coal and freight, and the suspension/delisting branch; it lands at Rp847, below the base of Rp1,028. The bull mirrors the shocks — a construction-led recovery, the free-float remedy passing, the Tuban terminal filling and a two-point margin recovery — and gives Rp1,235 [S17, S8, S14]. The probability-weighted value is Rp1,035, and the discounted target is Rp724.

What would change our view: a concrete free-float remedy that restores trading, which would remove the liquidity discount and make the fundamental value reachable; a visible upward reset in the related-party selling price, which would lift every forecast year; a sustained fall in the coal index below the deck, which would restore margin without needing price; and any sign that the parent intends to take the company private, which would put the appraised asset value of IDR30,573.2bn rather than the market price at the centre of the discussion [S20, S14].

Ownership is the whole story. Semen Indonesia holds 83.5%, the free float is 1.1%, and the exchange has suspended the shares for failing the free-float test [S9, S0, S16]. There is no independent block that could contest a resolution. The company's own disclosure of its delisting options — voluntary delisting, a rights issue with HMETD, a secondary offering of SIG's shares — is the clearest statement of where power sits: the controlling shareholder chooses the remedy and the minority receives it [S14]. Related-party dealings are not an exception here, they are the business: 91.2% per cent of FY2025 revenue came from related parties and IDR1,910.4bn of trade receivables were owed by them [S2]. We checked the filing for pledges of the controller's shares and found none disclosed, and for guarantees to affiliates outside the group and found none material [S2]. The auditor is Deloitte, whose opinion on the FY2025 accounts is unmodified [S2]. The board and management are disclosed in the pack; the finance and operations directors are the two executive seats that matter for this business [S0].

The dividend record is respectable and, for a state-owned group, predictable: a rising distribution through FY2024 and 36.5 a share out of FY2025 profit, with a stated policy of paying optimally subject to financial condition rather than a fixed ratio [S2, S10]. Payments have been about half of earnings, which is the assumption we carry [S2].

The structure flags are the ones the method card asks about. No special-monitoring board, but a special notation for the free-float shortfall, an active suspension, and a place on the exchange's forced-delisting watchlist — a status that breaks every entry and exit assumption, though the cause is ownership concentration rather than disclosure failure [S16, S18, S14]. No serial rights issues, no discounted placement to affiliates, no auditor down-tier [S2]. The one structural feature a minority should price is that the controlling shareholder is also the customer, so group policy on transfer pricing, on capital allocation and on the delisting route is set by a party whose interests are not aligned with the free float.

On ESG, cement is a carbon-intensive business and the exposure is regulatory and reputational rather than immediate financial. SMCB runs a sustainability roadmap to 2030, substitutes waste-derived fuel for coal in its kilns, and reports that sustainable solutions contributed a large share of revenue with carbon intensity down against its baseline [S4]. Alternative fuel is the one decarbonisation lever that also cuts cost, which is why we treat it as an operating advantage rather than a compliance cost [S11].

Cement emissions are process emissions as much as energy emissions: most of the carbon in a tonne of clinker
comes from calcining limestone, not from the fuel. That makes the industry's abatement path depend on clinker
substitution — blending more fly ash, slag or limestone into the cement — and on carbon capture for the
remaining clinker. For a producer, blending is cheap and capture is not, so the near-term response across the
region has been to raise the blending ratio and to burn waste.

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter: the two-year suspension threshold early next year, the FY2026 accounts in March, the dividend decision in June and the government construction programmes moving into execution through next year [S14, S11, S2, S17]. The one undated catalyst dominates them all — the exchange's decision on the free float and the company's choice among delisting, a rights issue and a secondary offering, which is the gate to everything else [S16, S14].

Between updates we watch five things. Volume against the national market, because SMCB's nine-month volume of 9.2 Mt sits against market growth of 7.8% and share loss is the quiet risk [S4, S17]. The realised price per tonne, because it is the only evidence of what the group is willing to pay for SMCB's cement. The related-party revenue share, because a fall would mean the company is being pushed into a spot market that is oversupplied [S2]. The coal index against the deck's US$52.5/t, because every dollar on the index moves cost of revenue before it moves price [S0]. And the register — any filing on the three remedies, because a rights issue, a placement or a delisting would change the share count and the value of everything else in this report [S14].

The company reports annually with interim and nine-month filings; the FY2026 interim accounts are already registered and show the June balance-sheet position, against which our FY2026E revenue of IDR11,451.5bn and gross margin of 21.7% will be tested [S3, S4]. We will update on the FY2026 accounts unless a free-float event or a related-party price reset arrives first.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Volume
assumptions.basis: FY2025A cement and clinker sales of 12.1 Mt [S11] on 14.86 Mt of installed cement capacity [S9]. FY2026E 12.38 Mt is the 9M2026 actual 9.17 Mt [S4] plus the FY2025 Q4 volume of 3.21 Mt (12.1 Mt less the 8.89 Mt nine-month base implied by the 3.16% growth in S4), with no Q4 uplift assumed; the >300,000 t shipped to the US west coast by September [S4] sits inside that run-rate. FY2027-29 grow at the 3.0% sales-volume growth the company itself uses in its value-in-use test [S2 p.56] and FY2030 at 2.0% as the 14.86 Mt ceiling is approached: 13.80 Mt is 93% utilisation and the 1.0 Mt Tuban terminal [F21] is therefore only about 0.6 Mt full in the base case; the remaining 0.4 Mt of export capacity is a bull-case driver.

assumptions.label: Average price
assumptions.basis: FY2025A realised Rp10,737bn on 12.1 Mt = Rp887k/t [S2, S11]. FY2026E Rp925k/t is the nine-month realised rate (Rp8,480bn on 9.17 Mt) carried into Q4 with no mix haircut [S4]: the export volumes earn a lower price and Q4 freight mix is not disclosed, so we treat the actual as the best estimate rather than shade it; the coal-linked component of price is carried separately through link1. FY2027-30 escalate at 2.5% a year, the sales-price growth the company assumes in its own impairment model [S2 p.56], so the long-run price is nominal, not a trough print.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025A 22.51% [S2], held flat in nominal terms rather than cut: 9M2026 gross margin is 22.2% on the same running revenue base [S4], so there is no evidence of margin decay to model. The coal and oil links below then move the printed margin with the decks, which is why FY2026E prints ~21.9% while ICI4 is 53% above its FY2025 average and recovers as the deck falls.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Coal and coal-linked power are the single largest cash cost of a clinker line. At roughly one tonne of clinker per 0.75 t of cement, ~0.10 t of thermal coal per tonne of cement at ICI4-equivalent grades puts the merchant coal bill near IDR 1.0-1.2trn, about 13-15% of the IDR 8,321bn cost of revenue [S2]; we use 15% after the coal-linked share of grid power. The rest of the cost base is limestone, maintenance, labour, distribution and the leases already in COGS.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Net of substitution and contract lag, 90% of a coal move is recovered. Evidence: ICI4 FY2026E 62.0 vs FY2025A 40.56 is a 53% jump, and over the same period SMCB lifted realised price per tonne ~4% while the gross margin rose to 22.2% [S4] on alternative-fuel substitution and cost programmes [S11]. The residual 10% is the true earnings sensitivity to coal.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Oil enters through distribution diesel, mining and mobile equipment and explosives: about 5% of cost of revenue, well below coal [S2]. Freight is a large cost line for a four-plant archipelago network, but most of it is contracted in rupiah per tonne rather than indexed to Brent.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: 85% recovered: diesel surcharges are reset with distributors more quickly than coal is repriced, so the oil link is a smaller residual earnings lever than coal. An asymmetric pass-through is not assumed in the opposite direction; bear and bull shock volume and price symmetrically.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The last actual is 1H2026, where distribution and selling of IDR 619,846 plus G&A of IDR 145,418 on revenue of IDR 5,502,337 is 13.91% [S3]; the nine-month reported figures imply 13.3-13.5% [S4]. The jump from 11.98% in FY2025 is outbound freight (domestic alone up 24% to IDR 470,970), new export freight and a step-up in other distribution costs, while G&A was flat [S3]. We hold 13.4%, the nine-month run-rate, in real terms for all five years: freight scales with volume, a constant share of revenue is the neutral assumption, and the company's "efisiensi operasional" narrative is not yet evidence of a lower reported ratio [S3, S4].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK: depreciation and depletion of fixed assets and quarry was IDR 660.3bn in FY2025, 6.15% of revenue [S2 note 12], not the IDR 9.9bn the data pack carries. Held flat: capex at 6.15% of revenue equals that charge so the asset base is held steady. Right-of-use depreciation of IDR 114.5bn [S2 note 13] is deliberately NOT added back: we treat the leases as operating costs, so the ROU charge is the proxy for the cash rent and the lease liabilities are excluded from the bridge (bank loans only, IDR 1,142.8bn at 30 June 2026 [S3]). Adding the ROU charge back gives IDR 1,867.1bn, matching the company's own "EBITDA sebesar Rp 1,87 triliun" [S11].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Steady state: capex is set equal to the depreciation charge so the 15.4trn rupiah asset base is held flat. FY2025 capex was only 3.6% of revenue after a Rp550bn programme, against 6.4% in FY2024 and 6.5% in FY2023 [S0], but a four-plant 14.86 Mt network cannot be maintained for less than its own depreciation charge, and a model that shrinks the asset base while growing revenue 4% a year overstates free cash flow. No expansion capex is assumed; the Tuban export terminal was funded at group level [S8].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(nwc, revenue))

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt))

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Engine default: three-year average of interest expense over opening total debt, 7.85%. The engine applies that rate to opening debt in every forecast year, so interest does not fall with the debt-repayment path the balance sheet shows: bank loans are already down to IDR 1,142.8bn at 30 June 2026 [S3] and net debt turns negative late in the forecast, so the convention overstates FY2027-30 interest expense and is conservative for value by a small, one-directional amount per share. The cash yield of 2.43% is credited on opening cash on the same convention. Left at the engine default rather than hand-set because the effect is second-order and does not move the rating, which the suspension rule fixes.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_income, cash[-1]))

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero: the company is paying debt down (loans interest fell from IDR 221bn in FY2024 to IDR 137bn in FY2025 [S2 note 31]) and has run no new facility beyond short-term working-capital lines, so the balance sheet is held, not re-levered. Any future draw is a financing decision, not an operating assumption.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero forward. FY2025 carried a foreign-exchange loss of IDR 30.3bn and other-net of IDR 7.5bn below the operating line [S2]; the FX loss is a translation item that reverses with the rupiah and other-net has no operating driver and averaged a small net charge over FY2024-25 [S2, S4]. They are held at zero rather than extrapolated so the forecast EBIT is an operating number; the LK's actual EBIT of IDR 1,092.3bn is used for history, so the reader can see the difference.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np))

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Fifty per cent: the FY2024 profit of IDR 745.1bn carried IDR 372.5bn of dividends [S2 statement of changes in equity, note 33], and the FY2025 profit of IDR 658.7bn carried Rp36.518 a share [S0], the same 50%. Held at 50% rather than the three-year average, which is dragged down by the FY2022 26% payout.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: engine default constant

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Two and a half per cent, exactly the perpetuity growth the company uses in its own value-in-use calculation on nominal rupiah cash flow [S2 p.56]. An industry at ~46% overcapacity with flat pricing [S6] has no case for real terminal growth, so we take the company's own rate rather than a house premium above it; 2.5% is below nominal GDP and above zero.

challenges.challenge: S14 (Kontan, 23 July 2026) is in fund record and cited nowhere in the report. It records that BEI announcement Peng-S-00019/BEI.PLP/06-2026 of 30 June 2026 lists 59 issuers at risk of forced delisting and that SMCB's corporate secretary says the company is considering voluntary delisting, a rights issue with HMETD, and a secondary offering of SIG's existing shares. The equity's terminal outcome is a live binary the report never states: section 5 frames a take-private only as an upside catalyst and section 7's 'undated catalyst' is the free-float decision alone. A 12-month target of Rp836 is not the most likely outcome for a register that may be extinguished or diluted.
challenges.answer: S14 now cited with its date; section 5 sets out voluntary delisting, HMETD rights issue and SIG secondary offering, their share-count and register effects, and the two-year delisting clock; frontmatter catalyst added. [S14]

challenges.challenge: opex_pct is set to 11.5% of revenue for all five forecast years, below FY2025A (1,286,574/10,737,250 = 11.98%) and far below 1H2026, where distribution and selling of 619,846 plus G&A of 145,418 on revenue of 5,502,337 is 13.91% [S3]. The 9M2026 article the analyst uses for revenue and volume implies 13.3-13.5% (gross profit 1,880 [F12] less an EBIT of about 736 back-solved from net profit 476.69 [F11]). Re-running the engine at 11.92% gives target Rp814 and TR 10.1%; at 13.9% it gives Rp708 and TR -4.9%. The ADD rating is produced by 42bp of unsourced opex efficiency, and the basis note's own cited trend (10.5%, 11.1%, 11.9%) is rising, not falling.
challenges.answer: opex_pct reset to 13.4% from 1H2026 distribution 619.846 plus G&A 145.418 on revenue 5,502.337, held flat for five years; section 3 explains the freight jump and states the total-return effect. [S3, S4]

challenges.challenge: The headline is ADD with a 13.2% total return on a stock that has not traded since January 2026: the pack shows adtv_3m_value_idr 0.0 and 63 zero-volume days, S16 puts SMCB on BEI's free-float suspension list (reguler dan tunai), and section 5 itself says 'a fundamental target is a marker rather than an exit'. fund rules line 309 defines the scale as 'NOT RATED: suspended / insufficient data', and fund record sets NOT RATED when the master status is suspended - but coverage/universe/idx_master.csv row 816 still carries SMCB.JK status 'listed' as of 2026-11-08, so the branch never fires and the report publishes an actionable-looking ADD.
challenges.answer: Master status set to suspended, engine re-run, rating prints NOT RATED per fund record; the investment summary keeps fundamental value and return as context only. [S16, S0]

challenges.challenge: The lease is charged twice. The bridge net debt of 1,141.259 is built from debt of 1,318.517, which is exactly bank loans 1,142.759 (769,097 current maturities + 373,662 long term) plus lease liabilities 175.758 (89,804 + 85,954) at 30 June 2026 [S3]. But the depreciation add-back is 660.342 only, excluding the 114.494 of right-of-use depreciation charged inside cost of revenue (105,756) and G&A (8,738) [S2 note 13], and therefore already inside the model's EBIT. The assumptions note says the model keeps ROU depreciation 'out of both free cash flow and the lease liability' - the second half is factually wrong. Adding it back moves the target from 836 to 921 (TR 24.1%) in the engine.
challenges.answer: Double count removed by the second route: ROU depreciation stays out of DA and lease liabilities out of the bridge via bs_debt 1,142.759 at 30 Jun 2026; adding ROU back reconciles to company EBITDA 1,870.0. [S2, S3, S11]

challenges.challenge: The report says 'EV/EBITDA at 6.7 times our FY2026E EBITDA gives Rp1,215', but the model applies 6.731475x to FY2025A EBITDA of 1,796.929 (6.731475 x 1,796.929 - 1,141.259 = 10,954.7, / 9,019.4 = 1,214.6). On the stated FY2026E EBITDA of 1,872.63 the same multiple gives Rp1,271, so the reader is given a basis the model does not use. The multiple is also described as 'our own through-cycle view' when it is mechanically the average of the peer median (4.89x) and the own five-year average (8.57x) under config multiple_source: blend; neither component is disclosed.
challenges.answer: EV/EBITDA prose now states FY2025A EBITDA 1,752.7, the blended multiple and the peer-median and own-history components, and why the leg is the most optimistic of the three. [S0]

challenges.challenge: The P/BV leg is presented as a 'book floor' and is not one. At 0.551938x it is the average of a peer median of 0.327x and an own five-year average of 0.777x, and it sits above the multiple the report's own argument implies: with ROE 5.5%, g 3.0% and COE 12.7%, justified P/BV is (0.055 - 0.03)/(0.127 - 0.03) = 0.26x, about Rp378 a share on book of 1,460. The report states 'a business earning a mid-single-digit return on equity should not trade at book' and then keeps 15% weight on a multiple 2.1x the justified level, saying it stops 'the DCF from running away'. At the peer median the leg contributes ~Rp350, not Rp806.
challenges.answer: Justified P/BV from ROE, g and COE stated as a fraction of book; the 0.55x blend is reconciled to the appraised asset value against book and described as a carrying-value floor, not a peer premium. [S20, S2]

challenges.challenge: The scenarios cannot test the thesis. Bear and bull shock only volume and price at 0.96/1.04 in FY+1, worth Rp1,134 and Rp1,257 against a base of 1,194 - a +/-5% band - while the engine's own sensitivity grid shows gross margin +/-2pp moving the target from 1,040 to 1,348, 2.5x the whole scenario range. The shocks are weak because the model has no operating leverage: cogs and opex are both percentages of revenue, so a volume shock cuts costs proportionally. Section 5 asserts the opposite ('a price cut of a few per cent passes almost entirely to EBIT') and then excuses the result ('the DCF is insensitive at the margin'). Doubling the bear probability gives TP 826 and TR 11.9% - still ADD, because the bear has no teeth.
challenges.answer: Bear and bull now carry mirrored gross-margin plus/minus 2pp shocks as well as volume and price plus/minus 4%, and both narratives include the free-float and delisting branch; probabilities 25/50/25. [S14, S3]

challenges.challenge: FY2026E net profit of 738.66 against 9M2026 actual of 476.69 [F11] implies Q4 2026 net profit of 261.97, versus 184.7 in Q4 2025 - a 42% year-on-year jump - on a Q4 gross margin of 20.2% against the 9M actual 22.2%. The full year grows 12.1% when the nine months grew 0.6% ('sedikit meningkat ... Rp474 miliar', S4). The report instead says it has 'not assumed a fourth-quarter deterioration beyond normal seasonality', which understates what the model assumes.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now shows the Q4 build explicitly (residual revenue at the 9M realised price, opex 13.4%, depreciation 6.15%, FY2025 debt cost, effective tax) and states the implied Q4 is below Q4 2025. [S4, S2]

challenges.challenge: The export channel is called 'the strategic novelty' and the 'one route by which SMCB can convert excess grinding capacity into volume', yet it is not in the base case: FY2030 volume of 13.99 Mt is 94% of the 14.86 Mt installed base [F15], growth is capped at the company's 3.0% VIU rate, and the Tuban terminal's 1.0 Mt capacity [F21] is never filled. Management began shipping in June 2026 and had moved more than 300,000 tonnes to the US west coast through the Taiheiyo partnership by September [S4] - an annualised ~0.6-0.9 Mt the model treats as ordinary volume. Because capex is held equal to depreciation, that upside needs no capital.
challenges.answer: Base case now states 13.8 Mt FY2030 is 93% utilisation and the Tuban terminal is only about 0.6 Mt full, with the residual 0.4 Mt kept as a bull driver and exports inside the 9M run-rate. [S4, S8]

challenges.challenge: The appraised asset value is the strongest upside in the report and is never valued. The appraiser put fixed assets at IDR30,573.2bn on 30 September 2024 against book of IDR15,429.0bn [S20, F29], a 2.0x gap the summary and section 5 both invoke - section 5 says a take-private 'would put the appraised asset value of IDR30,573.2bn rather than the market price at the centre of the discussion'. No method, no bridge item and no cross-check uses it, and the 0.55x P/BV leg works against it. On the industry card's own logic (through-cycle NAV of the assets) this is the natural fifth cross-check.
challenges.answer: Section 4 adds the asset cross-check: appraised PPE less net debt, a one-third overcapacity haircut, compared with the DCF and excluded from the weighted target with reasons stated. [S20]

challenges.challenge: Nine |pctv placeholders print ratios 100x too small, because pctv is documented in fund record as 'value already in percent' while the keys hold fractions. The rendered text includes 'We hold the gross margin input at 0.2%' (22.51%), 'we fund capex at 0.1% of revenue' (6.15%), 'which we carry forward at 0.5%' (50%), 'the 0.3% discount we then apply' (30%), 'terminal growth is 0.0%, a little above the two and a half per cent perpetuity' (3.0%) and 'Scenario probabilities of 0.2% bear, 0.5% base and 0.2% bull' (25/50/25). The terminal-growth sentence is a self-contradiction in the signed text.
challenges.answer: Every |pctv on a fraction key switched to |pct; render checked, ratios print 22.5%, 6.2%, 50.0%, 2.5%, 30.0% and scenario probabilities correctly. [S0]

challenges.challenge: Section 3 states 'Operating expenses of IDR1,280.0bn took EBIT to IDR1,136.6bn', but the LK shows operating expenses of 1,324.3bn (distribution 977,202 + G&A 309,372 + FX loss 30,256 + other-net 7,498) and profit before interest and tax of 1,092,308. The 44.3bn difference is the FX/other line, which the model routes to other_nonop and then zeroes for every forecast year - a normalisation never stated and carrying no qc_justification. That is exactly the -0.43pp calibration gap the gate reports and leaves open.
challenges.answer: Section 3 reconciles the LK operating lines with new facts F30-F35 to LK EBIT 1,092.3; zeroing FX and other-net forward is justified in the other_nonop basis and qc_justifications. [S2]

challenges.challenge: The report names the related-party transfer price as the first of the two things that move the value, then declines to quantify any downside: 'We model the last actual margin and neither assume a gift nor a haircut.' With 91.22% of revenue from related parties [F16] and IDR1,910.4bn of related-party receivables [F26] - 18% of revenue and 89% of the receivables book - a 2% downward reset is ~IDR230bn of revenue and, at the model's flow-through, roughly Rp60-70 a share. The bear scenario does not contain it and a DJP transfer-pricing adjustment is not mentioned.
challenges.answer: Bear scenario now quantifies a transfer-price reset and margin squeeze to 846.9 against a 1,028.3 base; related-party receivables are treated as a one-off cash use, not capitalised. [S2, S4]

challenges.challenge: Unmirrored conservatism in the financing lines. Interest expense is pinned at 146.33 for FY2026E-FY2030E (FY2025 total debt of 1,863.8 x 7.8513%) although the model's own net debt falls to -707.4 by FY2030 and 30 June 2026 debt is already 1,318.5 [S3]; no interest income is credited on the growing cash balance and net_borrowing is zero. Net profit, DPS and the 5.5% ROE the P/BV argument rests on are all understated, and the error grows every year.

findings.finding: The cost-of-capital paragraph in section 4 cannot be reproduced from its own stated inputs: 7.45% risk-free plus 1.0148 beta on (4.23% mature ERP + 2.46% country premium) is 14.2%, not the 12.6% printed. The gap is the engine's 1.62pp sovereign default spread subtracted from the government yield before the beta term (fund record coc: coe = rf - spread + beta*(erp+crp)), and the report discloses it nowhere.

The opex basis and section 3 both attribute a nine-month opex ratio of 13.3-13.5% to S4, which states no opex figure: it gives revenue 8,480, gross profit 1,880, net profit 476.69 and volume 9.17 Mt [S4]. The 13.4% input - the one the analyst says is worth more than the rating - is an unstated derivation, and it sits 0.5pp below the freshest actual, the 1H2026 LK's 13.91% [S3].

Related-party trade receivables are quoted at IDR1,910.4bn (31 December 2025) in sections 3, 5 and 6, but the valuation balance-sheet date is 30 June 2026, where the filing shows IDR2,122.1bn [S3] - 11% higher, and the H1 increase is itself evidence on the parent's payment behaviour.

Section 4 calls the P/BV leg '0.6 times forward book'. The 0.551938x is applied to FY2025A book of IDR1,464 a share to give 806; on FY2026E book it would be nearer 826. The multiple is trailing, not forward.

The FY2026E conservatism is disclosed but not sourced: the model prints a 21.7% gross margin and 14.4% EBITDA margin against 9M2026 actuals of 22.2% and roughly 14.9% implied, which forces a 2.2pp Q4 margin fade. No filing or deck explains why H2 2026 is worse than H1 2026 on flat volume at the same realised price.
Section 3 states that adding right-of-use depreciation of IDR114.5bn to 1,752.7 'gives IDR1,870.0bn'. It gives 1,867.1; the company's Rp1,87trn is rounded [S11].
